phase1.intro:
Every object you've built since Unit 1 has been living alone — one at a time. The moment you need more than one of something, you need somewhere to put them.

Where should we start?

topics.buttonText: Why isn't there just one "best" container?
dialogue: Think of the storage room out back — shelves, bins, filing cabinets. [[warn:There's no single "best" container]]. A shelf that stays in load order is great until you need to find one item fast. Every collection in Java is a trade-off someone already thought through — your job is learning which trade-off fits which job.

stickyNote.flavor: 🗄️ every collection is a deliberate trade-off
stickyNote.definition: There's no single best collection — each one (List, Set, Map, and their implementations) trades speed, order, or uniqueness differently.

topics.buttonText: What are the three main shapes — List, Set, Map?
dialogue: [[term:List]] — ordered, allows duplicates, a numbered shelf where position matters. [[term:Set]] — no duplicates, membership is the whole point, a guest list. [[term:Map]] — key-value pairs, a filing cabinet you look things up in by label.

stickyNote.flavor: 🗂️ ordered shelf, guest list, filing cabinet
stickyNote.definition: List: ordered, allows duplicates. Set: no duplicates, membership-focused. Map: key-value pairs, looked up by label.

topics.buttonText: Why are ArrayList and HashSet different from List and Set?
dialogue: [[fun:Every one of these is an interface, not a class]] — List, Set, and Map are promises about behavior, and ArrayList, LinkedList, HashSet, TreeMap are the actual storage rooms that keep those promises, each built differently under the hood.

stickyNote.flavor: 🤝 List is a promise, ArrayList keeps it
stickyNote.definition: List/Set/Map are interfaces — behavior promises. ArrayList/HashSet/TreeMap etc. are concrete implementations that fulfill those promises differently.

phase1.openingDialogue: The Collections Framework is Java's family of storage interfaces — List, Set, and Map, each a different trade-off for a different job. 🗄️

phase2.explanation:
Conceptual lesson — no broken code!

Common misconception: "I should always use ArrayList because it's the most popular."

Actually: ArrayList isn't always the best choice! If you're frequently inserting/deleting at the beginning of a list, LinkedList would be more efficient.

Example:
• ArrayList: O(1) for get, O(n) for insert at beginning
• LinkedList: O(n) for get, O(1) for insert at beginning

Choose based on your specific use case!

Another misconception: "HashSet is faster than TreeSet."

Actually: HashSet is O(1) for operations, TreeSet is O(log n). If you need sorted order, TreeSet is your only choice, but if you don't need order, HashSet is faster.

phase3.openingDialogue: Collections — choose the right container for the job! 📦

mcq.question:
Which collection should you use for:

"A list of students where you frequently need to access students by their ID number"

A) ArrayList
B) LinkedList
C) HashSet
D) HashMap

Select the BEST choice.

phase5.trivia: The Collections Framework was overhauled in Java 2 (1998) — before that, Java only had the clunky Vector and Hashtable classes, both fully synchronized (thread-safe but slow) by default. Modern List/Set/Map implementations dropped that automatic locking, which is exactly why [[warn:you'll need actual synchronization strategies of your own once this unit reaches multithreading]].
